items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: I joined Russell's orchestra... and Higgy who was the only one I knew... we were both happy to see each other after the year we had been with Helvey

ctx.x: Higginbottom's brother-in-law belonged to a lodge (the Elks I think it was) and through him we started playing for some of the dances the lodge would give at their meeting hall which was over a drug store at 6th and John Street. It was a famous market street, especially on Saturday. It was also part of the red light district. The street where one could hear the latest Bessie Smith records blasted over a loud speaker from early morning until late in the night.

Higginbottom was ahead of the rest of us as far as style was concerned. I had not heard many trombone players then. The few that I had heard never played the way Higgy did. I never knew who his inspiration could have been but he had been inspired by someone. All that I can say is that Higgy could blow better than anyone else in the orchestra.

We did quite a few dance jobs for the Elks at their hall and some dance jobs at the only negro hotel on Walnut Hills. Naturally we all felt very proud to be able to play for dancers. But we were not learning to read very well and John Coleman could not read at all. Nevertheless we had our repertoire and enjoyed playing our solos the best that we could.
